Good afternoon everybody. To continue our series about nutrients and health
Today, we will talk about curcumin.
We will take a look at some studies on the link between this substance and our health.
As many of you may know, curcumin is the vivid yellow orange substance that gives the
root turmeric its distinctive colour.
A member of the ginger family, turmeric has long been a staple of Indian culture consumed
including curries or prescribed as a natural remedy for illnesses.
Turmeric contains no more than 5% curcumin, but even such a low concentration of the
nutrient consumed regularly can address ailments from inflammation and depression to cancer
and dementia.
Although curcumin has long been used in traditional medicines, recent clinical trials
have given it the stamp of scientific approval.
Studies show that curcumin stimulates the release
of proteins called cytokines that calm and heal inflammation.
Chronic inflammation plays a role in many illnesses,
including cardiovascular disease, diabetes,
obesity, dementia, and depression.
Psychologist Adrian Lopresti,
a senior researcher at Murdoch University in Australia,
has conducted clinical trials of curcumin
as a treatment for depression.
The reason behind his trials is that since there's a lot
of evidence that people with depression
have greater levels of inflammation and oxidative stress,
curcumin can be used to improve mental health.
Other studies show that curcumin also guards the aging brain,
shielding against cognitive decline
and protecting against proteins linked to dementia.
A seemingly obvious example is in rural India.
This area has one of the lowest rates of Alzheimer's disease
which may be a clue to curcumin's protective role.
More recently, researchers have investigated
curcumin's role in generating and maintaining
Mitochondria, the part of human cells that are especially critical for brain power.
Studies show that curcumin contributes to the structural integrity of mitochondria
and their function. Mitochondrial dysfunction is strongly implicated in such neurodegenerative
conditions as Alzheimer's disease. In Australia, Andrew Scholle, the Director
of the Centre for Human Psychopharmacology at Swinbourne University in Melbourne, previously
found that daily consumption of a supplement containing 80 milligrams of curcumin boosted
memory and mood after four weeks. Now his team has extended the findings by observing
its influence over a longer period. The researchers gave 80 healthy adults aged 50 to 80 either
curcumin or a placebo once a day for three months. Participants completed questionnaires
that measured their emotional state and cognitive performance when the study began after four
weeks and again after 12. At the end of the study, those who consumed the
curcumin performed significantly better on three tasks of working memory than
those who received a placebo. Working memory reflects the ability to hold
information in the mind for ready retrieval, like remembering whose phone
number to dial after picking up the phone to make a call. Curcumin also
boosted participants moods, although the duration of the effect varied. Those who consumed curcumin
reported reductions in anxiety, anger and confusion after 4 weeks. But after 12 weeks
of taking the supplement, the benefit disappeared.
Curcumin's influence on fatigue were more sustained. The curcumin group reported less
exhaustion than the placebo group after both 4 weeks and 12.
The differences in the duration of effects suggest that curcumin works through multiple
mechanisms, Scully says.
Memory and mood are consistently the two most pressing concerns for his elderly patients.
As people get older, he finds they wish for stronger memory and more energy.
A daily dose of curcumin may be enough
to make a difference on everyday tasks.
Reaction times on memory tasks
may improve by only small margins, milliseconds,
but the moments gained can make a difference.
10 or 15 milliseconds don't mean that much to most people.
However, if you're driving a car, it could save your life.
